Question five. How does a random forest work? It's bagged trees with one more twist: at every split, a tree may only look at a random handful of features, here five of thirty. The trees stop all making the same cuts, so their mistakes overlap less, and the average gains more. On a hundred seventy-one held-out tumors, one tree scores ninety point six percent, bagged trees ninety-three, and the forest ninety-five point three. Question six. How does gradient boosting differ from AdaBoost? Gradient boosting fits each new tree to the gradient of the loss, the residuals for squared error, so any differentiable loss will do. AdaBoost, short for adaptive boosting, re-weights the data instead: after every round, the points it got wrong count for more. After three rounds, this point carries thirty-five times the weight of the easiest ones. AdaBoost turns out to be gradient boosting with an exponential loss. Back to the border that bent with the data.

Question seven. How does k-nearest neighbors, or K N N, make predictions? It keeps every training point. For a new one, it finds the k closest, and takes a vote. Here, fifteen neighbors, ten against five. There's no training step, but prediction is slow on large data. And k sets the trade-off. At k equals one, every point owns a patch of its own: a hundred percent on the training points, seventy-nine on new ones. At fifteen, the border is smooth, and scores ninety-three. At seventy-five, it's nearly straight, and drops to eighty-seven. Small k is high variance, large k high bias, so choose it by cross-validation. Neighbors need labels. Without them, you cluster.
